rv.q: The best thing about this play is that it’s positioned precisely at this intersection of comedy and pain.
Lane as the tortured soul at the play's heart is magnificent -- showing sides that are charming, witty, savage, self-destructive and yearning.
One of the most exciting things that a well-produced play can do is serve as a time machine, giving modern-day audiences a privileged glimpse of a corner of the lost world of the past.
Nathan Lane gives a performance of such depth and humanity that it transforms what could have been a standard backstage weepie into something genuinely moving.
Lane, in the apotheosis of his sad clown routine, is sensational throughout.
Nathan Lane gives a powerhouse performance in Douglas Carter Beane's moving drama
Mr. Lane gives what may be the performance of his career, finding the aching soul within the seemingly debased comic stereotype.
With his hunger to entertain and his precision timing, Lane reminds us why he’s a vaudevillian master in those scenes.

So even when material lets him down, which it finally does in 'The Nance,' Douglas Carter Beane's splendidly ambitious but psychologically superficial tragicomedy, it's thrilling to watch Lane bond with a character who demands the full attention of so many gifted layers of him.
Douglas Carter Beane has written a play that's both hilarious and heartbreaking, examining the cost of hiding one's true self in a world that demands conformity.
But after a steady diet of Broadway plays that are all about dysfunctional and sitcom-style families, “The Nance” is a welcome departure.
Even if the play eventually loses momentum, it is the most ambitious and substantial effort made to date by Beane.
Lane gets his juiciest comedic role since 2001's 'The Producers' but ultimately turns dark
Like Chauncy's two worlds, Beane's eventually crumble as well.
Lane's three-dimensional portrait of Chauncey Miles -- named after George Chauncey, whose 1994. Gay New York Beane consulted for background info -- is never a let-down.
I spent most of “The Nance” fascinated by the subject matter but frustrated by Beane’s execution.
Beyond that, things get a little murky.
What’s amazing about this scene is Lane is hilariously funny while he breaks our hearts.
A thoughtful and compassionate study in the forgotten ways of the metropolitan world of the last century, 'The Nance' is a flawed yet rich play that offers a great deal of heartbreak and hilarity.
